slides.title: Equations with Variables on Both Sides
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today: equations with the variable on both sides.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Q4 is today's move in miniature: taking 5x from 2x leaves −3x, and taking 2x from 5x leaves 3x. Say that in one sentence after the reveal — it is why Notes II takes the smaller x-term. Two minutes silent, then reveal, no discussion.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Two words, and the second is today's habit. A solution is not just the last line: it is the number that makes the two sides equal, so it is proved by putting it into BOTH sides of the first equation and getting the same number twice.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
The equation has x on both sides, so the first move is new: take 3x from BOTH sides. A balance stays level only if both pans lose the same thing — 3x from one side alone would tip it. What is left, 2x + 2 = 10, is Unit 1's two-step equation. Then the check, in both sides of the first equation: 5(4) + 2 = 22 and 3(4) + 10 = 22. The same number twice is the proof.
OFF: 'Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other — and that includes taking away x's.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
The same equation, two routes. Take 2x from both sides: 9 = 4x − 11, add 11, divide by 4. Take 6x instead: −4x + 9 = −11, subtract 9, divide by −4. Both give 5, because each step is done to both sides. The first route is easier: taking the smaller x-term leaves a positive coefficient, so no division by a negative. Check: 2(5) + 9 = 19 and 6(5) − 11 = 19.
OFF: 'Take the smaller x-term and the coefficient stays positive.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Parentheses are distributed before any term moves — yesterday's move first, today's second. The 3 multiplies the x AND the 4: 3x + 12. Then take 3x (the smaller) from both sides: 12 = 2x − 2. Then two steps. Check: 3(7 + 4) = 33 and 5(7) − 2 = 33.
OFF: 'Clear the parentheses, then move one variable term.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Ask which variable term is smaller before anyone writes: 4x. Take it from both sides.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Take 4x from both sides: 3x − 5 = 13. Then two steps: add 5, divide by 3. Check in both sides of the first equation: 7(6) − 5 = 37 and 4(6) + 13 = 37. A board with x = 18/11 added the x-terms (11x = 18); one with x = 8/3 took the 5 the wrong way.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Take 5x from both sides: 3x − 9 = 15, so 3x = 24 and x = 8. This catches a student who watched the move without doing it — a board with 13x = 24 added the x-terms; one with x = 2 subtracted the 9 (3x = 6).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: Parentheses first; a solution that is not whole.
slides.note: Ask what the 2 multiplies before anyone writes: the 3x AND the −1.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Distribute: 6x − 2. Take 4x from both sides: 2x − 2 = 9, so 2x = 11 and x = 5.5. A solution need not be a whole number — 5.5 is checked like any other: 2(16.5 − 1) = 31 and 4(5.5) + 9 = 31. A board with 2x = 10 distributed to one term (6x − 1).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 8x − 12 = 6x + 1, so 2x − 12 = 1, 2x = 13 and x = 6.5. This catches the one-term distribution: a board with 8x − 3 = 6x + 1 gets x = 2. Check: 4(13 − 3) = 40 and 6(6.5) + 1 = 40.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: One move, then one step. A board with x = 3.5 added the x-terms (8x = 28); one with x ≈ 4.67 dropped the 2x (6x = 28). Check in both sides: 42 = 42.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Notes I with bigger numbers. A board with x = 11 added the 4 (4x = 44); one with x ≈ 2.57 added the x-terms (14x = 36).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: The pattern breaks: the larger n-term is on the right, so the constants end on the left and the solution is negative. A board with n = 5 lost the sign of −20; one with n = 1 added 12 to −8 (4 = 4n). Check: −23 = −23.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. Option D adds the x-terms, option C moves the 8 the wrong way, option A drops the sign. On a split: sixty seconds, convince your neighbor, re-vote — then check −6 in both sides: −22 and −22.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Notes III's order: parentheses first, then a variable term. A board with x ≈ 3.67 wrote 2x + 7 (one term); one with x ≈ 3.33 took the 4 the wrong way (10 = 3x). Check: 2(6 + 7) = 26 and 5(6) − 4 = 26.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic: two of the three wrong options are the one-term distribution — on both sides (A) or on the right only (B). Option D adds the x-terms. Ask a room that chose C to check 9 in both sides: 28 and 28.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: The extra-number board (ruling 22): the gym's 7 days a week is not needed. Each plan's cost is an expression in v; the two plans cost the same when the expressions are equal, 30 + 5v = 8v. Take 5v (the smaller) from both sides. Check: both plans cost \$80 at 10 visits.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Backwards: the solution is given and a number in the equation is missing. Put 3 in for x on BOTH sides — the right side is 22, the left is 15 + □. Check: 5(3) + 7 = 22 and 2(3) + 16 = 22.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and the exit evidence. Read two aloud: one that names the reason (the same step done to both sides), one that checks 6 in both sides. Lena divides by −4 — the room that forgets the sign gets −6, and the check exposes it: 2(−6) + 15 = 3, 6(−6) − 9 = −45.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in writing.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set; the same six questions are on the board. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.
